title: Joseph’s Brothers Bow in Egypt
summary: Famine drives ten brothers to Egypt, where they bow before Joseph unrecognized; he tests them, their consciences awaken, Simeon is held, and Jacob refuses Benjamin.
historicalContext: More than twenty years have passed since the brothers sold Joseph at Dothan. He was seventeen then (37:2), became Pharaoh’s chief minister at thirty (41:46), and seven years of plenty have run their course, so he is now in his late thirties. The famine he foretold has reached Canaan, where pastoral families depended on seasonal rain, while Egypt, watered by the Nile and stocked by Joseph’s granaries, has grain to sell. Semitic travellers going down to Egypt to buy food in hard years appear in Egyptian records and art, and the eastern border was watched closely, since Asiatic groups had more than once slipped into the Delta and seized power. A charge of spying against ten armed foreigners arriving together was therefore plausible. Oaths by the life of the reigning king are attested in Egyptian texts, and the use of an interpreter fits a court where a high official addressed foreigners only through intermediaries.
literaryContext: Genesis 42 opens the long movement (chs. 42–45) in which the family torn apart in chapter 37 is brought back together. The chapter begins and ends in Canaan with Jacob withholding Benjamin “lest mischief befall him” (vv. 4, 38), and the words “live, and not die” (v. 2) are answered by the shadow of “the grave” (v. 38). At the centre stand two audiences in Egypt. Language from chapter 37 returns with reversed force: the brothers who would not “hear” their pleading brother now hear themselves judged; the verb “know” or “recognize,” once used to deceive Jacob with the bloodied coat, now describes Joseph seeing through his brothers while they fail to see him; and silver, the price of Joseph’s sale, turns up in their sacks. The dreams of sheaves and stars begin to come true as ten men bow, yet the eleventh is missing, and the narrative presses on toward the moment when Joseph makes himself known.
themes: The awakening of a guilty conscience
Testing that seeks repentance, not revenge
A divided family moving toward reconciliation

outline.title: Jacob Sends Ten Sons to Egypt
outline.summary: With famine in Canaan, Jacob rouses his sons to go down and buy grain so the family may live, but keeps Benjamin at home for fear of harm.

outline.title: The First Audience: Bowing and Accusation
outline.summary: The brothers bow before the governor, fulfilling Joseph’s dreams; recognizing them, he hides himself, charges them as spies, demands their youngest brother, and confines them three days.

outline.title: Conscience Awakened
outline.summary: Joseph eases the terms because he fears God; the brothers confess their guilt toward Joseph, Reuben speaks of blood required, Joseph weeps in secret and binds Simeon.

outline.title: Silver in the Sacks
outline.summary: Joseph sends them home with grain, provisions, and their money restored; finding silver in one sack, the brothers tremble and ask what God has done to them.

outline.title: Jacob Refuses to Send Benjamin
outline.summary: The brothers report to Jacob, find all their money returned, and hear their father’s lament; he rejects Reuben’s rash pledge and will not let Benjamin go.

verses.bibleText: Now when Jacob saw that there was corn in Egypt, Jacob said unto his sons, Why do ye look one upon another?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene shifts from Pharaoh’s court back to Canaan, where the famine Joseph foretold has reached Jacob’s tents. “Now when Jacob saw that there was corn in Egypt” uses the ordinary verb for seeing, though Jacob has not travelled south; he “saw” in the sense of learning from reports and perhaps from caravans returning with grain. News of Egypt’s stores had spread through the region, for “all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn” (41:57).

Jacob’s question to his sons, “Why do ye look one upon another?”, catches a family frozen in helplessness. The ten sons stand staring at each other while their households go hungry. The men who once acted with such cunning against Joseph (37:18-20) and against Shechem (34:25-29) now seem paralysed. Some have suggested that the very name of Egypt touched a nerve, since it was to Egypt that they had sold their brother. The narrator does not say so, but the hesitation sits uneasily beside what follows.

The old patriarch is the one who acts. Though his grief over Joseph had never healed, he still bears responsibility for the clan and takes the initiative. Behind his decision lies a larger hand. The famine is the instrument by which God will bring the whole family to Joseph, fulfilling the dreams and preserving the line of promise (45:5-7). The psalmist puts it plainly: God “called for a famine upon the land” after he had “sent a man before them, even Joseph” (Psalm 105:16-17).

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבֶר (shever) — corn
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes grain offered for sale, and the related verb in verses 2-3 means “to buy grain.” It is a different word from the general term for food used in verse 7. The vocabulary is commercial: Egypt had become the region’s granary, and Jacob’s sons go as buyers, carrying silver (v. 25). The same word describes the grain Joseph sold to all lands (41:56-57), and Amos later pictures greedy merchants eager to sell it at inflated prices (Amos 8:5).

wordNotes.term: תִּתְרָאוּ (titra’u) — look one upon another
wordNotes.explanation: A reflexive form of the verb “to see,” meaning to stare at one another. Here it portrays men who are idle and perplexed, each waiting for another to move. Elsewhere the same form describes kings who “look one another in the face” as they prepare to meet in battle (2 Kings 14:8), but in this setting the sense is passive bewilderment rather than challenge.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Behold, I have heard that there is corn in Egypt: get you down thither, and buy for us from thence; that we may live, and not die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob repeats the news, as if his sons need to be told twice: “Behold, I have heard that there is corn in Egypt.” Then comes the command, “get you down thither, and buy for us from thence.” Going down to Egypt in famine was a pattern in the family. Abraham went in a time of hunger (12:10), and Isaac was about to go when the Lord told him to stay in the land (26:1-2). Jacob plans no migration, only a buying trip, perhaps because he did not expect Egypt’s supplies to last for strangers.

The purpose clause carries the weight of the verse: “that we may live, and not die.” The stakes are survival. Life and death run through the whole chapter and the next. Judah will use almost the same words when he urges Jacob to release Benjamin (43:8), and Joseph will tell his brothers, “This do, and live” (v. 18). The family that carries the promise of blessing to all nations is at the point of starvation, and the seed of Abraham seems as fragile as it has ever been.

Hungry and anxious, the household does not know that the bread it seeks is in the hands of the brother it sold. The one rejected has become the source of life, and the only way to live is to go to him. Jesus spoke of himself in comparable terms: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (John 6:35).

wordNotes.term: וְנִחְיֶה וְלֹא נָמוּת (venichyeh velo’ namut) — that we may live, and not die
wordNotes.explanation: The pairing of a positive verb with its negated opposite stresses that the alternative is death. Judah repeats the formula word for word (43:8), and the Egyptians use it when they offer themselves to Pharaoh for food (47:19). Moses later sets the same choice before Israel in covenant terms: life and good, death and evil (Deuteronomy 30:15, 19).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph's ten brethren went down to buy corn in Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph’s ten brethren went down to buy corn in Egypt.” The narrator could have called them Jacob’s sons, as in verse 1, or the sons of Israel, as in verse 5. Here they are “Joseph’s ten brethren.” The title reminds the reader of the relationship they had betrayed and points toward the meeting ahead. They go to buy bread; they are about to meet their brother.

All ten went. Each was head of a household by now, and a larger party could buy and carry more grain. A group also offered protection on a long road through dry country where hungry raiders might target a caravan of food. The journey from Hebron to the Egyptian Delta was about a week by donkey.

The number matters for the dreams. In Joseph’s first dream eleven sheaves bowed to his (37:7). Ten are on their way. The bowing will begin in this chapter, yet the full picture waits until Benjamin also comes. God’s word is moving toward fulfilment step by step, through ordinary choices made under the pressure of hunger.

wordNotes.term: אֲחֵי־יוֹסֵף עֲשָׂרָה (achei-yosef ‘asarah) — Joseph’s ten brethren
wordNotes.explanation: The brothers are named in relation to Joseph, the brother they no longer mention by name. In chapter 37 they called him “this dreamer” and “the child” (37:19, 30), avoiding his name. The narrator here restores the bond they denied. When Joseph later reveals himself, he will say, “I am Joseph your brother” (45:4).

verses.bibleText: But Benjamin, Joseph's brother, Jacob sent not with his brethren; for he said, Lest peradventure mischief befall him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, Jacob sent not with his brethren.” The narrator again calls Benjamin “Joseph’s brother,” for he and Joseph were the only sons of Rachel. Benjamin is not a small boy. If Joseph is now near forty, Benjamin is probably in his twenties, and by the time the family moves to Egypt he has ten sons (46:21). Jacob keeps him home for a different reason: “Lest peradventure mischief befall him.”

The fear is revealing. Benjamin has taken Joseph’s place in his father’s heart. Jacob had sent his favourite out once before, to check on his brothers at Shechem, and Joseph never came back (37:13-14, 32-33). He will not repeat that loss. Whether Jacob suspected the ten is left unsaid. His protectiveness echoes his old preference for Rachel’s children, the very favouritism that once stirred the brothers’ hatred (37:3-4). The household has not yet been healed.

This detail will become the hinge of the whole story. Joseph will notice Benjamin’s absence, demand his presence, and finally test whether the brothers will abandon Rachel’s other son as they abandoned him. The word “mischief” forms a frame around the chapter, returning in Jacob’s last speech (v. 38) and in Judah’s plea (44:29).

Jacob guards Benjamin with human caution, unaware that the safety of the whole family depends on letting him go. God’s purposes sometimes require loosening the very grip by which people try to secure what they love.

wordNotes.term: אָסוֹן (’ason) — mischief
wordNotes.explanation: The word means a harmful accident or fatal calamity. In Genesis it occurs only in Jacob’s fear for Benjamin (vv. 4, 38) and in Judah’s retelling of it (44:29). Outside Genesis it appears in the law about injury to a pregnant woman, where “if no mischief follow” means no serious or fatal harm (Exodus 21:22-23). Jacob fears that Benjamin might suffer the fate he believes befell Joseph.

verses.bibleText: And the sons of Israel came to buy corn among those that came: for the famine was in the land of Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the sons of Israel came to buy corn among those that came.” The brothers arrive as part of a stream of foreigners pouring into Egypt for food. They may have travelled with a caravan or simply joined the crowds at the border. Nothing marks them out. They are one hungry group among many.

The name “sons of Israel” is significant. The phrase will become the name of the nation, and the book of Exodus opens with the same words: “these are the names of the children of Israel, which came into Egypt” (Exodus 1:1). Here the family enters Egypt as a small, troubled clan seeking bread. Generations later its descendants will leave as a great people.

The closing clause, “for the famine was in the land of Canaan,” explains why the heirs of the promised land are found outside it. God had told Abraham that his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own (15:13). Hunger is the means God uses to move them, and it falls on Canaan as on every other country.

wordNotes.term: בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (benei yisra’el) — the sons of Israel
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “sons of Israel,” using the covenant name God gave Jacob at Peniel (32:28). In this narrative it refers to the eleven brothers, but the same phrase becomes the standard name of the nation, translated “children of Israel.” The list of those who came into Egypt is introduced with it (46:8), and Exodus opens by repeating that list (Exodus 1:1).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph was the governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land: and Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator pauses to set the stage: “And Joseph was the governor over the land, and he it was that sold to all the people of the land.” The slave sold for twenty pieces of silver now controls the food supply of the known world. The title “governor” stresses real power, the authority of one whose word is decisive, and agrees with Pharaoh’s grant in 41:40-44. That Joseph personally oversaw the sales, at least to foreigners, may reflect careful control of the stores in a time of crisis, and perhaps also a hope that his family would one day appear.

Then comes the moment the story has been moving toward since chapter 37: “and Joseph’s brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth.” They prostrate themselves in the ordinary manner of petitioners before a great official. They have no idea that they are fulfilling the dream they mocked. “Shalt thou indeed reign over us?” they had asked (37:8). Now they lie on the ground before him, and they do it of their own accord, to gain the grain that will keep them alive.

The word “earth” or “land” appears three times in the Hebrew of this verse: Joseph rules over the land, sells to the people of the land, and his brothers bow with their faces to the land. The repetition sets the one exalted over the land beside those pressed into its dust.

The scene displays the certainty of God’s word. Twenty years of silence, slavery, and prison did not cancel what God had shown Joseph in his dreams. The brothers tried to kill the dream by getting rid of the dreamer (37:20), yet their efforts became the road to its fulfilment. Joseph would later say, “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (50:20). The pattern is seen most fully in Christ, rejected by his own and exalted to the place of authority, before whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9-11).

wordNotes.term: הַשַּׁלִּיט (hashshallit) — the governor
wordNotes.explanation: From a root meaning “to have mastery” or “to rule.” The noun describes one who holds effective power. Ecclesiastes uses it of power no one has over the day of death (Ecclesiastes 8:8), and the related verb describes the dominance of enemies in Esther (Esther 9:1). The word is later familiar in the Arabic title sultan. Here it confirms that Joseph wields the authority Pharaoh delegated to him.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁתַּחֲווּ־לוֹ אַפַּיִם אָרְצָה (vayyishtachavu-lo ’appayim ’artsah) — bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to prostrate oneself, and the added phrase “nostrils to the ground” describes full prostration. It is the same verb used in Joseph’s dreams of the sheaves and of the sun, moon, and stars bowing (37:7, 9). Abraham’s servant used it in worship of the LORD (24:26), but here it expresses submission to a human ruler. The brothers will bow again on their second visit (43:26, 28).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them, and spake roughly unto them; and he said unto them, Whence come ye? And they said, From the land of Canaan to buy food.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph saw his brethren, and he knew them, but made himself strange unto them.” Recognition is instant. Joseph knows the faces, the dress, the speech of his own kin. He chooses at once to conceal himself. The Hebrew sets two forms of the same root side by side: he recognized them, and he made himself unrecognizable. The verb recalls the brothers’ own deception, when they brought Joseph’s bloodstained coat to Jacob and said, “know now whether it be thy son’s coat or no” (37:32). They once used recognition to deceive their father; now the brother they sold uses non-recognition to search their hearts.

He “spake roughly unto them,” literally “spoke hard things with them.” The question “Whence come ye?” is the routine interrogation of a border official, but delivered harshly. Why this severity? The narrative does not portray Joseph as vindictive. He weeps more than once during these encounters (v. 24; 43:30; 45:2), and he provides for them throughout. His harshness serves a purpose: he needs to discover whether these are still the men who threw him into the pit, and what has become of Benjamin, whose absence he immediately notices. Revealing himself at once would have produced fear and pretence, not truth.

The brothers answer simply: “From the land of Canaan to buy food.” It is true, and it is all they mean to say. They have no idea how much more the man before them already knows.

Joseph’s concealment is a unique instrument in a unique situation, not a pattern for deceiving others. He holds the power of life and death over men who once held such power over him, and he uses it with restraint, aiming at their restoration. Scripture shows God dealing in similar ways, hiding his hand for a time so that hearts may be brought to repentance before he makes himself known (Isaiah 45:15; Hosea 5:15).

wordNotes.term: וַיַּכִּרֵם וַיִּתְנַכֵּר (vayyakkirem vayyitnakker) — he knew them, but made himself strange
wordNotes.explanation: Both verbs come from the root nakar. The causative form means “to recognize,” and the reflexive form means “to make oneself unrecognized,” to act as a stranger. The root runs through the Joseph and Judah stories: Jacob was asked to recognize the bloody coat (37:32-33), and Judah was asked to recognize his own seal and staff (38:25-26). Each time recognition exposes hidden guilt.

wordNotes.term: קָשׁוֹת (qashot) — roughly
wordNotes.explanation: The plural of an adjective meaning hard or severe, used adverbially: “hard things.” It occurs in this form only here and in the brothers’ report to Jacob (v. 30). The simpler form describes Rehoboam’s harsh answer to the people (1 Kings 12:13). Joseph’s words are stern, though the narrative shows that his heart is not hard.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him.” The narrator repeats the first half of verse 7 and adds the decisive contrast. Recognition runs only one way. The repetition slows the story at its turning point, letting the reader feel the gap between what Joseph sees and what his brothers cannot see.

Their blindness is easy to explain. They last saw Joseph as a youth of seventeen; he is now a grown man approaching forty. He wears Egyptian linen, is clean-shaven in the Egyptian manner (41:14), speaks Egyptian through an interpreter (v. 23), and sits in the seat of the most powerful official in the land. Even if a resemblance had crossed their minds, the idea that the brother they sold as a slave could be ruling Egypt would have seemed absurd. When he finally tells them, they are struck dumb (45:3).

The scene has a long echo in Scripture. The one who came to save was in the midst of his own and they did not know him. John writes of Christ, “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John 1:10-11). Stephen, recounting Joseph’s story before the council, notes that “at the second time Joseph was made known to his brethren” (Acts 7:13), and he presses the parallel: Israel had repeatedly failed to recognize the deliverers God sent (Acts 7:25, 35).

wordNotes.term: וְהֵם לֹא הִכִּרֻהוּ (vehem lo’ hikkiruhu) — but they knew not him
wordNotes.explanation: The same causative verb used for Joseph’s recognition in verse 7, now negated. Recognition and its failure are key motifs in these chapters. Isaac failed to recognize Jacob in disguise (27:23), and Jacob did not recognize the deception behind the coat. Now those who deceived are themselves unable to recognize. The disguise works because no one expects the rejected brother to be the lord of the land.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them, and said unto them, Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them.” The sight of his brothers on their faces brings the dreams flooding back. Joseph had named his first son Manasseh because God had made him forget his toil and his father’s house (41:51); now memory returns with force. He sees that the sheaves have bowed, just as God showed him more than two decades earlier. Yet only ten are here. Benjamin is missing, and in the second dream even his father and mother bowed (37:9-10). The dreams are beginning to come true, but not completely.

This remembrance shapes what Joseph does next. He does not recall the pit, the chains, or the silver; the narrator links his conduct to the dreams. That suggests his aim is to carry forward what God has revealed, leaving the old score unsettled: the reunion of the whole family under his care. Pharaoh’s dreams had led Joseph to a plan for saving Egypt; his own dreams now guide a plan to save his family, body and soul.

He charges them: “Ye are spies; to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.” Egypt was vulnerable on its eastern frontier, and in the past groups from Canaan and beyond had filtered into the Delta and even seized power there. Border fortresses were built to watch such movements. Ten foreign men of military age arriving together in a time of famine could plausibly be scouting for weaknesses in the defences or the grain stores. The accusation is a pretext, but a believable one.

The charge also turns the brothers’ past against them. Joseph had once been sent by his father to see how his brothers were faring (37:14), and they hated him as a talebearer who brought evil reports (37:2). Now they are accused of being men who come to spy out and report. They had falsely treated him as a threat; now they are falsely treated as one. Through this reversal they begin to taste, in measure, what they made their brother suffer.

wordNotes.term: מְרַגְּלִים (meraggelim) — spies
wordNotes.explanation: From a verb related to the word for foot, meaning to go about on foot, and so to explore or reconnoitre. The same verb describes the scouts Joshua sent to Jericho (Joshua 2:1) and David’s spies (1 Samuel 26:4). The accusation implies a military purpose: men walking the land to report its weak points to an invading force.

wordNotes.term: עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ (‘ervat ha’arets) — the nakedness of the land
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Ervah means nakedness or exposure, often in contexts of shame (9:22; Leviticus 18:6). Applied to a country, it describes undefended places, the gaps in its protection that an enemy could exploit. The figure pictures the land as exposed and vulnerable. Isaiah uses the language of nakedness for the humiliation of a conquered people (Isaiah 47:3).

verses.bibleText: And they said unto him, Nay, my lord, but to buy food are thy servants come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Nay, my lord, but to buy food are thy servants come.” The brothers protest at once, and the protest is cast in the language of deference. They call Joseph “my lord” and themselves “thy servants.” Whatever indignation they feel, fear makes them humble. Earlier they had refused to bow to Joseph even in imagination (37:8); now they address him as master with every sentence.

Their answer is the truth. They came to buy food, nothing else. Yet the irony is heavy. These men once called their brother a servant and sold him into slavery; now they style themselves servants before him. The words that bring them low are the words the dreams foretold, for Joseph’s brothers had asked in scorn whether he would indeed have dominion over them (37:8).

The exchange also shows how much power now rests with Joseph. One word from the governor could send these men to prison or to death, and they know it. Their humility is the humility of men with no other option. Whether it will become the humility of men who have changed is the question the rest of the story will answer. Outward bowing is easy under pressure; the test Joseph is about to set will probe for something deeper.

Jesus stated the principle that governs such reversals: “whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). The brothers had set themselves above the dreamer; now they are brought low before him. Yet the lowering is meant to lead somewhere better, for the God who humbles the proud gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5).

wordNotes.term: עֲבָדֶיךָ (‘avadeykha) — thy servants
wordNotes.explanation: The plural of ‘eved, servant or slave, used in polite self-reference before a superior. Jacob spoke of himself this way before Esau (32:4; 33:5). Here it gains irony because Joseph had been an ‘eved in Potiphar’s house (39:17). The brothers will end by offering to become Joseph’s servants in earnest (50:18).

verses.bibleText: We are all one man's sons; we are true men, thy servants are no spies.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The brothers press their defence: “We are all one man’s sons; we are true men, thy servants are no spies.” Their reasoning is sound. No father would send ten sons together on a dangerous espionage mission and risk losing his whole family at once. Spies came as individuals or small bands, not as a family of brothers. By stating their kinship they hope to remove suspicion.

The statement carries an irony they cannot see. “We are all one man’s sons” includes the man who stands before them. Joseph is also a son of that one man, the brother they do not mention, standing within earshot of their claim to family unity.

Their second claim cuts deeper: “we are true men.” The word means honest, upright, men whose word can be trusted. It is true in the present moment, for they have come only to buy food. But Joseph knows how these men once lied to their father about a torn coat and let him grieve for twenty years. Are they now men of truth? That is precisely what Joseph sets out to test. Their claim to honesty will be weighed in the coming chapters until Judah, offering himself in Benjamin’s place, shows that something has truly changed (44:33).

Scripture often uses the testing of words to expose the heart. “The heart is deceitful above all things,” and only God, the searcher of hearts, knows it fully (Jeremiah 17:9-10). The brothers will learn that being true men requires more than avoiding a single lie; it requires coming clean about the past.

wordNotes.term: כֵּנִים (kenim) — true men
wordNotes.explanation: The plural of ken, a word meaning right, firm, or so, from the same family as words for being established. As a description of people it means honest or upright, men whose words correspond to reality. The word recurs as a refrain in this chapter (vv. 19, 31, 33, 34). It also describes what is right or correct, as when the daughters of Zelophehad “speak right” (Numbers 27:7).

verses.bibleText: And he said unto them, Nay, but to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said unto them, Nay, but to see the nakedness of the land ye are come.” Joseph answers their emphatic “Nay” with one of his own and repeats his charge almost word for word. He offers no reasons and does not engage their argument. The hammering repetition is the method of an interrogator who wants to break down resistance and draw out more information.

It works. Pressed by a charge they cannot disprove, the brothers will say more than they planned, and in the next verse they mention the two brothers who are absent, the very subject Joseph most wants to hear about.

Joseph knows perfectly well that the charge is false. His insistence is part of a role he has chosen to play for a season, and the narrative is candid about it. It never invites readers to imitate such tactics in ordinary dealings. What it shows is the pressure under which hidden things begin to surface, as the brothers, unable to clear themselves, are driven back upon their family history.

wordNotes.term: לֹא כִּי (lo’ ki) — Nay, but
wordNotes.explanation: The combination of the negative with the adversative particle forms a sharp contradiction: “No, rather.” Sarah uses a similar construction when she denies laughing and the Lord answers, “Nay; but thou didst laugh” (18:15). The repetition of the brothers’ own “Nay” in Joseph’s reply turns their denial back on them.

verses.bibleText: And they said, Thy servants are twelve brethren, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and, behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Desperate to prove their innocence, the brothers enlarge their story: “Thy servants are twelve brethren, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan; and, behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is not.” They add details they think will make them more credible: the number of brothers, the homeland, the father still living, the youngest at home. In doing so they give Joseph exactly what he wants to know.

For Joseph, two pieces of news stand out. His father is alive, and Benjamin is alive and at home with him. He had not heard from his family in more than twenty years. Now, in a few words spoken by men who do not know him, he learns that Jacob still lives and that Rachel’s other son has not been harmed.

Then comes the phrase that must have struck Joseph to the heart: “and one is not.” They speak of him as dead or vanished, the brother no longer counted. They still number him among the twelve, which is perhaps a small sign that he has not been wholly erased from their minds. But the euphemism hides the truth. They do not say how he came to be “not.” The brothers who once said “the child is not” to explain his disappearance (37:30) now say it to the very brother they lost.

The count of twelve is itself significant. These twelve will become the tribes of Israel. Though one is missing and the family is scattered between Canaan and Egypt, God still sees them as twelve. Revelation pictures the people of God sealed under the names of those same tribes (Revelation 7:4-8). What the brothers count as lost, God counts as kept.

wordNotes.term: וְהָאֶחָד אֵינֶנּוּ (veha’echad ’enennu) — and one is not
wordNotes.explanation: The particle ’ein with a suffix means “he is not, he is absent.” It is used of Enoch, who “was not; for God took him” (5:24), and of Joseph when Reuben finds the pit empty: “The child is not” (37:30). Jacob will use it of both Joseph and Simeon (v. 36). The phrase leaves the fate of the missing one vague, which suits the brothers’ need to avoid the truth. Jeremiah echoes it in Rachel’s lament for her children, “because they were not” (Jeremiah 31:15).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto them, That is it that I spake unto you, saying, Ye are spies:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph said unto them, That is it that I spake unto you, saying, Ye are spies.” The brothers’ fuller explanation only seems to confirm Joseph’s suspicion. In his role as a hard official, he treats their mention of a brother left at home as further evidence: perhaps the father kept one son back because he knew the mission was dangerous.

The argument is closed. The brothers say nothing more, and Joseph moves from accusation to action. He has learned what he needs. Their story about Benjamin is now the point on which their honesty will be tested. Joseph has turned their own words into the condition of their release.

There is something fitting in the position the brothers now occupy. Twenty years earlier Joseph had pleaded with them and could not make them listen (v. 21); now they plead with a man who will not be moved by their protests. They cannot argue their way out. Only proof will do, and the proof they need is the brother who was left at home, the other son of Rachel whom their father guards so closely.

wordNotes.term: הוּא אֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתִּי (hu’ ’asher dibbarti) — That is it that I spake
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “It is what I said to you.” The pronoun points back to the charge already made, as though their extra information had settled the matter. When Jacob later rebukes his sons for telling the man about Benjamin, they explain that he questioned them closely about their family (43:7).

verses.bibleText: Hereby ye shall be proved: By the life of Pharaoh ye shall not go forth hence, except your youngest brother come hither.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Hereby ye shall be proved.” Joseph announces a test. The brothers have claimed to be true men; now their words will be examined against the facts. The proof he demands is specific: “ye shall not go forth hence, except your youngest brother come hither.” Only the appearance of the brother they described will show that their story is honest.

The demand reveals Joseph’s deeper concerns. He wants to see Benjamin with his own eyes. He has only their word that Rachel’s other son is alive and well, and these are the men who sold him and lied about it. He also wants to see how they will respond to a situation that places a favoured son of Rachel in their hands again. Will they guard Benjamin, or abandon him as they abandoned Joseph? The test that begins here reaches its climax in chapter 44, when Benjamin is accused of theft and the brothers must choose whether to go home without him.

Joseph backs his words with an oath: “By the life of Pharaoh.” Swearing by the life of the reigning king was a customary Egyptian formula, attested in inscriptions, and it fits the part Joseph is playing as a high Egyptian official. The Israelite equivalent was to swear by the life of the LORD (Ruth 3:13), sometimes joined to the life of the king (1 Samuel 25:26). The narrator records Joseph’s words without commending the form; the point is that the governor speaks with the full weight of the throne behind him.

The idea of proving runs throughout Scripture. God tested Abraham (22:1), and the psalmists invite God to try their hearts (Psalm 139:23). Peter speaks of the trial of faith as gold refined in fire (1 Peter 1:7). Testing exposes what is real. Joseph’s test is a human one, but it serves a divine purpose: to bring the brothers’ hearts into the light.

wordNotes.term: תִּבָּחֵנוּ (tibbachenu) — ye shall be proved
wordNotes.explanation: A passive form of bachan, “to examine, test, try.” The verb is often used of God testing the heart and mind (Jeremiah 17:10; Psalm 139:23), and of refining metal to show its quality (Zechariah 13:9). The brothers’ claim to honesty is to be assayed like silver. In verse 16 Joseph uses the same verb again: “that your words may be proved.”

wordNotes.term: חֵי פַרְעֹה (chei far‘oh) — by the life of Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: An oath formula: “as Pharaoh lives.” In Israel people swore “as the LORD liveth” (Judges 8:19; Ruth 3:13), sometimes adding the life of the king or of the person addressed (1 Samuel 25:26; 2 Samuel 15:21). The oath invoked the highest authority known to the speaker as guarantor of his word.

verses.bibleText: Send one of you, and let him fetch your brother, and ye shall be kept in prison, that your words may be proved, whether there be any truth in you: or else by the life of Pharaoh surely ye are spies.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph spells out the first form of his test: “Send one of you, and let him fetch your brother, and ye shall be kept in prison.” One man would return to Canaan; nine would remain confined until he came back with Benjamin. The demand was harsh. It meant months of imprisonment, starving families at home, and a father who would almost certainly refuse to let Benjamin go.

The purpose is stated plainly: “that your words may be proved, whether there be any truth in you.” Truth is the issue. The brothers have made claims about themselves; now those claims will be checked. If they fail, Joseph concludes with a second oath, “by the life of Pharaoh surely ye are spies,” and the penalty for spies was death.

There is a sharp irony in Joseph’s question about truth. The brothers had lived a lie for more than twenty years, deceiving their father about Joseph’s fate (37:31-35). They are honest about why they came to Egypt, but their lives rest on a buried falsehood. The question “whether there be any truth in you” reaches further than they realize. The God who desires “truth in the inward parts” (Psalm 51:6) is using this test to uncover the lie at the centre of their family.

wordNotes.term: הַאֱמֶת אִתְּכֶם (ha’emet ’ittekhem) — whether there be any truth in you
wordNotes.explanation: ’Emet means truth, faithfulness, reliability, that which can be depended upon. The question asks literally, “Is truth with you?” The word is used of God’s faithfulness to his promises (24:27; 32:10) and of the integrity God requires in the heart (Psalm 51:6). The brothers’ words will be measured against that standard.

verses.bibleText: And he put them all together into ward three days.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he put them all together into ward three days.” The brothers either refused the proposal of verse 16 or could not agree on who would go, so Joseph confines all ten. The word “ward” is the same used of the place where Pharaoh’s butler and baker were held with Joseph (40:3-4; 41:10). The brothers are likely placed in the same guardhouse where Joseph himself had spent years.

The parallel is unmistakable. Joseph had been thrown into a pit and left while his brothers sat down to eat (37:24-25), then sold and eventually imprisoned. Now the brothers sit in custody, not knowing whether they will live or die. Joseph’s confinement lasted years; theirs lasts three days. The measure is mild, far lighter than what they had inflicted. Yet three days in an Egyptian prison, accused of a capital crime, with no way to prove their innocence, gave them time to think.

What passed through their minds in those days goes unreported; verse 21 reveals the result. Somewhere in that confinement, memory awoke. The cries of a boy pleading from a pit came back to them. Suffering often has this effect. The psalmist could say, “Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word” (Psalm 119:67). God uses hardship to open eyes that comfort had kept closed.

The span of three days appears repeatedly in Scripture as a period of trial followed by deliverance. Joseph interpreted the butler’s and baker’s dreams in terms of three days (40:12-13, 18-19). Jonah was three days in the fish (Jonah 1:17), and Jesus spoke of his own three days in the heart of the earth before rising (Matthew 12:40). The brothers’ three days end with an offer of life.

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁמָר (mishmar) — ward
wordNotes.explanation: From shamar, “to keep, guard.” The noun means custody, a place of confinement under guard. It is used of the place where Pharaoh’s officers were held with Joseph (40:3-4; 41:10) and later of the custody in which a blasphemer or a Sabbath-breaker was held until the LORD’s will was known (Leviticus 24:12; Numbers 15:34).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto them the third day, This do, and live; for I fear God:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph said unto them the third day, This do, and live; for I fear God.” On the third day the tone changes. Joseph offers terms that open a way to life. The words “This do, and live” echo Jacob’s command to his sons, “that we may live, and not die” (v. 2). The brothers came to Egypt seeking life for their families; now the governor holds it out to them, conditioned on obedience to his word.

The reason he gives is striking: “for I fear God.” From the lips of an Egyptian official the phrase would have sounded like a general claim to piety, a statement that he was a man with a conscience who would not treat foreigners unjustly. The word for God is Elohim, not the covenant name, which suits his disguise. But to the reader, and perhaps to the brothers in time, the phrase means much more. Joseph truly fears God. It was the fear of God that had kept him pure in Potiphar’s house: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” (39:9). Abraham had once lied because he assumed there was no fear of God in Gerar (20:11). Joseph’s fear of God makes him trustworthy even to strangers.

The fear of God is also what the brothers had lacked when they dealt with Joseph. They saw his anguish and did not hear (v. 21). Fear of God restrains cruelty and opens the heart to compassion. Joseph’s statement implies a contrast: here is a man who will deal justly with you, as you did not deal with your brother.

The fear of the Lord is “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10) and the root of right conduct. Nehemiah, governing in a later age, refused to oppress the people “because of the fear of God” (Nehemiah 5:15). Joseph uses his power under the same restraint. His severity has a limit set by reverence for God, and that limit guarantees that his purpose is mercy, not destruction.

wordNotes.term: אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים אֲנִי יָרֵא (’et-ha’elohim ’ani yare’) — I fear God
wordNotes.explanation: Yare’ means “to fear,” and with God as its object it describes reverent awe that shapes conduct. The word order places God first for emphasis: “God I fear.” Abraham assumed that “the fear of God is not in this place” (20:11), and the midwives in Egypt later “feared God” and refused Pharaoh’s order to kill the Hebrew boys (Exodus 1:17). The fear of God is consistently linked with mercy toward the vulnerable.

wordNotes.term: זֹאת עֲשׂוּ וִחְיוּ (zo’t ‘asu vichyu) — This do, and live
wordNotes.explanation: Two imperatives joined, where the second states the result of obeying the first: do this, and you will live. The pattern recurs in the law, where keeping God’s statutes brings life (Leviticus 18:5), and Jesus used the same thought when he told the lawyer, “this do, and thou shalt live” (Luke 10:28).

verses.bibleText: If ye be true men, let one of your brethren be bound in the house of your prison: go ye, carry corn for the famine of your houses:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph reverses his first plan. Instead of keeping nine and sending one, he will keep one and send nine: “let one of your brethren be bound in the house of your prison: go ye, carry corn for the famine of your houses.” The change shows mercy. Joseph knows that their households in Canaan are starving. Holding nine men for months would have meant death for their wives and children. He tempers his test with compassion.

The condition is still framed around their honesty: “If ye be true men.” They had claimed this description (v. 11); now they must prove it. The brother left in prison becomes the pledge. If they do not return, he will die and their claim will be shown false.

The arrangement deliberately recreates a situation the brothers knew well. Once before they had gone home to their father without one of their brothers, leaving him in the hands of foreigners bound for Egypt. Now they must do so again. The question is whether they will treat this brother as they treated Joseph, or whether they will return for him at cost to themselves. This time they will. On the second journey they return with Benjamin, and Simeon is brought out to them (43:23).

wordNotes.term: רַעֲבוֹן בָּתֵּיכֶם (ra‘avon batteikhem) — the famine of your houses
wordNotes.explanation: Ra‘avon is a less common word for hunger or famine, used here and in verse 33 and once in the Psalms (Psalm 37:19), where the righteous are satisfied “in the days of famine.” “Houses” means households: wives, children, servants, and Jacob himself. Joseph’s concern for the hungry households shows that his test is not meant to destroy.

verses.bibleText: But bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die. And they did so.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But bring your youngest brother unto me; so shall your words be verified, and ye shall not die.” Joseph completes the terms. The release of the hostage, the clearing of their name, and their own survival all depend on Benjamin’s coming. The phrase “ye shall not die” repeats the life-and-death theme of the chapter. Joseph knows that the grain they carry will not last through years of famine. They must come back, and when they come, Benjamin must be with them.

“And they did so.” The brief note shows that they accepted the terms, apparently without further protest. The narrator may be summarizing ahead, since verse 24 records the actual selection of Simeon, but the point is clear: they submit. They have little choice. Yet the submission also marks a change. In chapter 37 they took matters into their own hands; now they bow to conditions set by another.

The word “verified” is related to the Hebrew root that gives us “amen.” Their words will be shown to be firm and reliable, or not. God’s own word is described in these terms: his promises are faithful and sure. The brothers’ words must now meet a test that their past would fail.

wordNotes.term: וְיֵאָמְנוּ (veye’amenu) — so shall your words be verified
wordNotes.explanation: A passive form of ’aman, meaning to be firm, reliable, confirmed. The same root describes Abraham believing God (15:6) and Solomon’s prayer that God’s word to David “be verified” (1 Kings 8:26). Here the brothers’ words must be confirmed by evidence. The noun forms of this root include “faithfulness” and the response “amen.”

verses.bibleText: And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother.” This is the heart of the chapter. In the presence of the governor, talking among themselves in Hebrew, the brothers confess. They do not mention spying or Egypt’s suspicion. They go straight to the wrong they had kept buried for more than twenty years. Without anyone naming it, conscience names it for them.

The phrase “said one to another” recalls the day they first plotted against Joseph: “they said one to another, Behold, this dreamer cometh” (37:19). The same men, using the same form of speech, once agreed on murder; now they agree on their guilt. Then they spoke as conspirators; now they speak as penitents.

Their confession is specific: “in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear.” Chapter 37 never mentioned Joseph’s pleading; the narrator held it back until now, so that the reader hears it for the first time through the brothers’ memory. The detail is haunting. They had watched a seventeen-year-old beg for his life from the bottom of a cistern and had sat down to eat bread (37:25). They saw his anguish, and they shut their ears. Now that memory surfaces with painful clarity. The sin was not only in what they did but in what they refused to hear.

Then comes the connection: “therefore is this distress come upon us.” The Hebrew uses the same word for Joseph’s “anguish” and their “distress.” They see a moral correspondence. The distress they caused has returned upon them. They do not know that the man before them is Joseph, but they recognize the hand of a higher justice. Paul states the principle: “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Moses would later warn, “be sure your sin will find you out” (Numbers 32:23).

This is the awakening Joseph’s test was designed to bring about. His harshness was not revenge; it was a means of reaching consciences that had grown hard. True repentance begins when sin is acknowledged as sin, without excuse. “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Godly sorrow, Paul writes, “worketh repentance to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The brothers have taken the first step on that road.

wordNotes.term: אֲבָל אֲשֵׁמִים (’aval ’ashemim) — verily guilty
wordNotes.explanation: ’Aval is an emphatic particle, “truly, indeed,” and ’ashemim is the plural adjective from ’asham, “to be guilty, bear guilt.” The root covers both the state of guilt and its consequences, and in the law it names the guilt offering required for wrongs against God or neighbour (Leviticus 5:15; 6:2-6). The brothers acknowledge that they stand guilty and liable. Isaiah later describes the Servant’s life as made an ’asham, an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:10).

wordNotes.term: צָרַת נַפְשׁוֹ … הַצָּרָה (tsarat nafsho … hatstsarah) — the anguish of his soul … this distress
wordNotes.explanation: Tsarah means distress, tightness, a narrow place of trouble. The brothers saw Joseph’s tsarah, and now tsarah has come on them; the repeated word binds crime and consequence. Nafsho, “his soul,” refers to Joseph himself as a living, feeling person in mortal danger, not to an immortal element within him. Jacob had spoken of God answering him “in the day of my distress” (35:3).

verses.bibleText: And Reuben answered them, saying, Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child; and ye would not hear? therefore, behold, also his blood is required.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reuben answered them, saying, Spake I not unto you, saying, Do not sin against the child; and ye would not hear?” Reuben breaks into the confession with a reproach. He reminds his brothers of the warning he gave at the pit. Chapter 37 records that Reuben talked them out of killing Joseph and had him thrown into the cistern instead, intending to rescue him later and return him to his father (37:21-22). He had been absent when the others sold Joseph and was distraught to find the pit empty (37:29-30).

Reuben’s words carry an edge of self-defence. Faced with shared guilt, he points out that he had argued against the crime. Yet his record is not clean. His plan to rescue Joseph was never carried out; he had gone along with the deception of their father; and he kept silent for twenty years while Jacob mourned. His good intentions did not keep his brother from slavery. Reuben’s rebuke adds to the brothers’ conviction, but it also shows how partial resistance to evil can leave a man sharing in its guilt. Still, his words confirm the main point: they had been warned, and “ye would not hear.” The refusal to listen runs through the confession like a refrain. They did not hear Joseph, and they did not hear Reuben.

Then comes his grim conclusion: “therefore, behold, also his blood is required.” Reuben assumes Joseph is dead, and he sees their present danger as God calling them to account for his life. The language recalls God’s word to Noah: “surely your blood of your lives will I require; at the hand of every man’s brother will I require the life of man” (9:5). The brothers had not shed Joseph’s blood with their own hands, but they had dipped his coat in goat’s blood and let their father believe he was dead. Now that pretended blood rises against them as a real accusation.

Cain had asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” and heard that his brother’s blood cried from the ground (4:9-10). The theme runs through Scripture: God does not forget the blood of the innocent. Hebrews contrasts Abel’s blood, crying for justice, with the blood of Jesus, which “speaketh better things” (Hebrews 12:24), the blood that brings forgiveness to those who have wronged their Brother.

wordNotes.term: דָּמוֹ הִנֵּה נִדְרָשׁ (damo hinneh nidrash) — behold, also his blood is required
wordNotes.explanation: Nidrash is a passive form of darash, “to seek, inquire, require.” With “blood” as its subject it means that an account is demanded for a life taken. God uses the active form in his covenant with Noah: “your blood … will I require” (9:5). Ezekiel applies it to the watchman whose silence leads to death: “his blood will I require at thine hand” (Ezekiel 3:18). Reuben believes the time of reckoning has come.

wordNotes.term: אַל־תֶּחֶטְאוּ בַיֶּלֶד (’al-techet’u vayyeled) — Do not sin against the child
wordNotes.explanation: Chata’ means to sin or offend, and with the preposition it names the person wronged. Yeled, “child” or “boy,” is the word Reuben used when he found the pit empty (37:30). Chapter 37 does not record this exact sentence, but Reuben’s earlier plea, “Let us not kill him” (37:21), carried the same intent.

verses.bibleText: And they knew not that Joseph understood them; for he spake unto them by an interpreter.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they knew not that Joseph understood them; for he spake unto them by an interpreter.” The narrator explains how the brothers could speak so openly in Joseph’s presence. Joseph had addressed them through an interpreter, keeping up the appearance of an Egyptian lord who knew no Hebrew. They assumed he could not follow their conversation. In fact he heard every word.

The use of an interpreter fits court custom. A high official would speak to foreigners through an intermediary, both for practical reasons and to maintain distance. For Joseph it also preserved his disguise. A slip into his native tongue would have given him away.

The verse places the reader beside Joseph. We hear what he hears: his brothers confessing their guilt, recalling his anguish, acknowledging that they would not listen. For the first time he learns that Reuben had tried to save him. For the first time he hears them speak of their sin without excuse. The man who had pleaded unheard now hears without being seen to hear.

There is a lesson here about the God who hears. People speak among themselves as though no one else is listening, yet “there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether” (Psalm 139:4). The brothers’ confession, spoken to one another, was heard by the one they had wronged. Confession of sin is never lost on the God who sees in secret.

wordNotes.term: הַמֵּלִיץ (hammelits) — an interpreter
wordNotes.explanation: A participle of a root associated with speaking for another, used of an intermediary or spokesman. In Job 33:23 it describes a messenger who mediates between God and man, “an interpreter, one among a thousand,” and in 2 Chronicles 32:31 the envoys of Babylon. Here it is a court interpreter standing between Joseph and his brothers.

wordNotes.term: שֹׁמֵעַ (shomea‘) — understood
wordNotes.explanation: The common verb for hearing, here meaning to understand speech. It ties into the chapter’s repeated theme: the brothers “would not hear” Joseph (v. 21) or Reuben (v. 22), but Joseph hears them. In the Tower of Babel account the same verb describes people unable to understand one another’s language (11:7).

verses.bibleText: And he turned himself about from them, and wept; and returned to them again, and communed with them, and took from them Simeon, and bound him before their eyes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he turned himself about from them, and wept.” The governor’s stern mask cracks. Hearing his brothers confess their guilt and remember his anguish, Joseph cannot hold back his tears. He turns away so they will not see. This is the first of several times Joseph weeps in these chapters. He will weep again at the sight of Benjamin (43:30), aloud when he reveals himself (45:2), on Benjamin’s neck (45:14-15), on his father’s neck (46:29), at Jacob’s death (50:1), and when his brothers beg forgiveness (50:17).

The tears reveal what the harsh words concealed. Joseph is not driven by bitterness. He grieves over his brothers, over the years lost, over the pain on every side. Perhaps he weeps also because he sees what he had hoped to see: a sign that his brothers were no longer the men who threw him into the pit. Their confession opened the way to reconciliation. His tears show the heart behind the test.

Yet Joseph does not stop the test. “And returned to them again, and communed with them, and took from them Simeon, and bound him before their eyes.” Remorse spoken among themselves is a beginning, but not yet proof. Joseph needs to see whether their sorrow will produce changed action, whether they will come back for Simeon and bring Benjamin safely.

Why Simeon? Reuben was the firstborn, and normally the eldest would be held. But Joseph had just learned that Reuben tried to save him. Simeon, the next in line, had shown his violence in the massacre at Shechem (34:25-30), and Jacob later rebukes his cruelty (49:5-7). He may well have taken a leading part in the plot against Joseph. Binding him “before their eyes” made the scene unforgettable. They had once bound their brother, or at least stripped him and thrown him into a pit, while he begged. Now they watch one of their own bound and led away.

Joseph’s conduct here models something of God’s ways. The Lord disciplines those he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and the discipline is real, yet behind it stands a heart moved with compassion. Hosea portrays God saying of rebellious Israel, “mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together” (Hosea 11:8). Jesus wept over Jerusalem even as he announced its judgment (Luke 19:41). Grief and firmness can dwell together in a love that seeks the full restoration of the one who has gone astray.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּבְךְּ (vayyevk) — and wept
wordNotes.explanation: From bakah, the ordinary verb for weeping. Tears mark Joseph’s story at every stage of reconciliation (43:30; 45:2, 14; 46:29; 50:1, 17). Esau and Jacob wept when they met after their long estrangement (33:4). The verb expresses grief, joy, and deep emotion together, and here it reveals the tenderness behind Joseph’s stern exterior.

wordNotes.term: וַיֶּאֱסֹר אֹתוֹ (vayye’esor ’oto) — and bound him
wordNotes.explanation: ’Asar means to tie, bind, or imprison. It is the root behind “the place where the king’s prisoners were bound” in which Joseph was confined (39:20) and is used of the brothers being held “in the house of your prison” (v. 19). Simeon now experiences what Joseph had known. Samson was later bound with fetters by the Philistines (Judges 16:21).

verses.bibleText: Then Joseph commanded to fill their sacks with corn, and to restore every man's money into his sack, and to give them provision for the way: and thus did he unto them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Then Joseph commanded to fill their sacks with corn, and to restore every man’s money into his sack, and to give them provision for the way.” Joseph gives three orders, each more generous than the last. Their containers are filled with grain. Their payment is secretly returned. They receive extra food for the journey, so that the grain for their families need not be touched on the road. “And thus did he unto them.”

Why return the money? The text does not say, and Joseph’s motives may have been several. He could not bring himself to take payment from his own father and brothers for bread. He wished to provide for them generously without revealing himself. He may also have meant the silver to press their consciences further. The money returned in their sacks would recall the silver they had taken for him: twenty pieces paid by the Ishmaelites at Dothan (37:28). Then they valued silver above their brother. Now they would carry home silver they had not earned and could not explain.

The returned silver also tests their honesty. Would they keep it in silence, or would they bring it back? On their second journey they bring it back, along with double money, and confess it to Joseph’s steward before they are asked (43:12, 20-22). That too is a sign of change.

The brothers leave Egypt carrying more than they paid for, without knowing it. The man they fear has treated them with grace. They do not yet see it as grace; to them it will look like a trap. But the pattern is the pattern of the gospel. God gives freely, without price (Isaiah 55:1), and his gifts are at first received with fear by those whose consciences accuse them. Only when the giver is revealed does the gift become joy. Paul says that “the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance” (Romans 2:4).

wordNotes.term: כַּסְפֵּיהֶם (kaspeihem) — their money
wordNotes.explanation: Kesef means silver, and since silver was weighed out as currency it also means money. It is the word used of the twenty pieces of silver paid for Joseph (37:28). Silver becomes a key word in chapters 42-45, appearing about twenty times. Abraham paid for the cave of Machpelah in silver weighed according to merchants’ standards (23:16).

wordNotes.term: צֵדָה (tsedah) — provision
wordNotes.explanation: Food for a journey, provisions for the road. The word appears when the Gibeonites show their dry, mouldy “provision” as proof of a long journey (Joshua 9:11), and when the Israelites left Egypt without having prepared “any victual” for the way (Exodus 12:39). Joseph supplies it freely, so that the grain bought for the households need not be opened on the road.

verses.bibleText: And they laded their asses with the corn, and departed thence.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they laded their asses with the corn, and departed thence.” The verse is brief and matter-of-fact. The brothers load their donkeys and start for home, nine men where ten had come. The grain they had come to buy is now theirs, but the journey back is heavy. Simeon remains bound in Egypt, and they must face their father with the news.

The narrator says nothing about their conversation on the road, but the silence speaks. The men who once sat down to eat after throwing their brother into the pit (37:25) now set out with food and a burden they cannot set down. They carry grain for life and guilt for a brother. They do not yet know that the silver for that grain lies hidden among it.

The donkeys laden with Egypt’s grain are the first of a series of caravans moving between Egypt and Canaan. Later Joseph will send wagons and donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt to bring his father down (45:23).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׂאוּ אֶת־שִׁבְרָם עַל־חֲמֹרֵיהֶם (vayyis’u ’et-shivram ‘al-chamoreihem) — they laded their asses with the corn
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “they lifted their grain upon their donkeys.” Shever is the same word for grain offered for sale used in verses 1-3. The chamor, the donkey, was the common beast of burden for such journeys. Abraham saddled his donkey for the journey to Moriah (22:3), and Joseph’s brothers will load their donkeys again on the second trip (44:13).

verses.bibleText: And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack's mouth.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money.” At the first stopping place on the road home, one brother opens a sack to feed his donkey and finds the silver lying at the top. The narrator does not name him.

The “inn” was a lodging place, probably a spot by the road where travellers camped for the night, perhaps near a well. There was no building or host. Each man looked after his own animals.

The discovery is abrupt and alarming: “for, behold, it was in his sack’s mouth.” The word “behold” marks the shock. The silver should have been in Egypt’s treasury. Instead it sits in plain view, as though placed there deliberately. The brothers had already been accused of being spies; now they could be accused of being thieves. They would not have to wait long for that fear to take shape (43:18).

In their later account to Joseph’s steward, the brothers say that all of them found their money at the lodging place (43:21). The narrator here records only one discovery on the road and the rest at home (v. 35). The brothers’ retelling compresses events, and the narrator lets both accounts stand.

wordNotes.term: מָּלוֹן (malon) — the inn
wordNotes.explanation: From the verb lun, to lodge or spend the night. A malon is a place to stop overnight, a campsite on a journey, not an inn in the later sense. The word is used of the lodging place where the LORD met Moses on his way to Egypt (Exodus 4:24) and of the place where the Israelites camped after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 4:3). The related verb describes Jacob spending the night at Bethel (28:11).

wordNotes.term: אַמְתַּחְתּוֹ (’amtachto) — his sack
wordNotes.explanation: ’Amtachat is a word used only in the Joseph story, appearing in chapters 42-44 alongside the more common saq, sack. It probably denotes a large bag or travelling sack. Joseph’s cup will later be hidden in Benjamin’s ’amtachat (44:2, 12), the climax of the test that begins with this silver.

verses.bibleText: And he said unto his brethren, My money is restored; and, lo, it is even in my sack: and their heart failed them, and they were afraid, saying one to another, What is this that God hath done unto us?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said unto his brethren, My money is restored; and, lo, it is even in my sack.” The brother calls out to the others, and his words tumble out in disbelief. The silver has been returned; there it is, in his own sack. He cannot explain it and dares not keep it hidden.

“And their heart failed them, and they were afraid.” Literally, “their heart went out.” Courage drains away. They turn trembling to one another. The silver should have been good news, but to men whose consciences are already raw it can only mean trouble. They have been accused of spying; now they look like thieves. On their return, the governor could seize them all. And behind the human danger they sense something greater.

“Saying one to another, What is this that God hath done unto us?” For the first time in the whole Joseph story the brothers speak of God. In chapter 37 they plotted, deceived, and profited without a word about him. Now, confronted by an inexplicable event, they see the hand of God. The confession of verse 21 has opened their eyes. They do not interpret this as chance or as the trick of a corrupt official; they see it as God dealing with them.

Their question echoes earlier questions in Genesis. God asked Eve, “What is this that thou hast done?” (3:13). Pharaoh and Abimelech asked Abraham and Isaac the same thing when deception was exposed (12:18; 26:10). Laban asked Jacob, “What is this thou hast done unto me?” (29:25). Now the brothers ask what God has done to them. Yet the question implies the other. They know that their own deed lies behind God’s dealings.

Their fear is the fear of guilty men. They cannot yet see that the silver is a gift. The same providence they dread is working for their good. Joseph will later say, “God did send me before you to preserve life” (45:5). What looks to them like the hand of judgment is the hand of mercy bringing them, by a hard road, to reconciliation.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּצֵא לִבָּם (vayyetse’ libbam) — their heart failed them
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “their heart went out.” The idiom describes a loss of courage or a sinking of spirit. The heart in Hebrew thought is the centre of thought, will, and emotion. A similar picture appears when the hearts of the Canaanites “melted” at the news of Israel’s coming (Joshua 2:11) and when the soul of the Shulamite “failed” at her beloved’s word (Song of Solomon 5:6).

wordNotes.term: מַה־זֹּאת עָשָׂה אֱלֹהִים לָנוּ (mah-zo’t ‘asah ’elohim lanu) — What is this that God hath done unto us?
wordNotes.explanation: The construction “What is this …?” appears repeatedly in Genesis when hidden wrong comes to light (3:13; 12:18; 29:25). Here the brothers, rather than an injured party, ask it, and they name God as the actor. Their question shows awakened conscience: they read their circumstances as God’s response to their guilt.

verses.bibleText: And they came unto Jacob their father unto the land of Canaan, and told him all that befell unto them; saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And they came unto Jacob their father unto the land of Canaan, and told him all that befell unto them.” The journey home passes in a single clause. The narrator moves straight to the moment the brothers dread: facing their father with Simeon missing.

They tell him “all that befell unto them,” yet the report that follows is selective. They say nothing of the three days in custody, nothing of Simeon being bound before their eyes, nothing of their confession of guilt over Joseph or Reuben’s words about blood, and nothing yet about the silver found at the lodging place. “All” means all they think their father needs to hear. They shape the account to soften the blow and to make the case for sending Benjamin.

The brothers had once brought Jacob a report built on a lie (37:32). This report is truthful in what it says, but careful in what it leaves out. Their concern now seems to be for their father’s feelings, a small but real change from the callousness of twenty years before.

wordNotes.term: הַקֹּרֹת אֹתָם (haqqorot ’otam) — that befell unto them
wordNotes.explanation: A participle of qarah, “to meet, happen, befall.” It describes events that come upon someone, often unexpectedly. A closely related verb expresses Jacob’s fear that harm might “befall” Benjamin (vv. 4, 38), and Mordecai told Esther “all that had happened unto him” (Esther 4:7). The brothers report what has happened to them, as though they were only the objects of events.

verses.bibleText: The man, who is the lord of the land, spake roughly to us, and took us for spies of the country.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The man, who is the lord of the land, spake roughly to us, and took us for spies of the country.” The brothers begin with the governor. They do not name him, calling him only “the man,” and they stress his power: he is “the lord of the land.” The title will be repeated in verse 33, as if to impress on Jacob that they had no choice in dealing with such a figure.

Their description repeats the narrator’s own word from verse 7: he “spake roughly” to them, using the same rare plural form. They felt the hardness of his words keenly. To their father they portray the governor as harsh and suspicious, and themselves as innocent victims of his suspicion.

What they leave out is as telling as what they include. They do not say that he imprisoned all of them for three days, or that he swore twice by the life of Pharaoh. They present the accusation as a misunderstanding rather than a capital threat. Their retelling aims to calm their father, not alarm him, since they will need his consent to return.

The irony continues. “The man” whom they describe with such awe is the son Jacob mourns. The words “lord of the land” fulfil Joseph’s dreams, and the brothers speak them to the very father who once rebuked Joseph for dreaming that his family would bow to him (37:10).

wordNotes.term: הָאִישׁ אֲדֹנֵי הָאָרֶץ (ha’ish ’adonei ha’arets) — the man, who is the lord of the land
wordNotes.explanation: ’Ish is the ordinary word for a man, and ’adonei ha’arets, “lord of the land,” uses the plural form of ’adon, “lord, master,” to express majesty. The brothers will continue to call Joseph “the man” in their arguments with Jacob (43:3, 5-7). When Joseph reveals himself, he will say that God has made him “lord of all his house, and a ruler throughout all the land of Egypt” (45:8).

verses.bibleText: And we said unto him, We are true men; we are no spies:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And we said unto him, We are true men; we are no spies.” The brothers repeat their protest to their father. In verse 11 they had said, “we are true men, thy servants are no spies.” Now, before Jacob, they drop the deferential “thy servants” and state their innocence more confidently. In front of the governor they were humble; at home they are bolder.

Their insistence on being “true men” is important to them, and they repeat it in the presence of the one man they have deceived for twenty years. Jacob hears his sons call themselves honest. He has no idea that the deepest lie of their lives concerns him. The reader cannot hear the phrase without remembering the bloodied coat.

Yet there is also hope in the claim. Honesty is now something they value and want to be known for. The test Joseph has set will show whether that claim can become the truth about their whole history as well as their trip to Egypt.

wordNotes.term: לֹא הָיִינוּ מְרַגְּלִים (lo’ hayinu meraggelim) — we are no spies
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “we have not been spies,” using the perfect tense of the verb “to be.” The form denies that they have ever been spies, a stronger statement than a simple present denial. A matching form appeared in their original protest, “thy servants have not been spies” (v. 11). The participle for spies is the same used of Joshua’s scouts (Joshua 6:22).

verses.bibleText: We be twelve brethren, sons of our father; one is not, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“We be twelve brethren, sons of our father; one is not, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.” The brothers repeat what they told the governor, with small but revealing changes. Before Joseph they said they were “the sons of one man” (v. 13). Before Jacob they say “sons of our father.” The phrase draws the circle tight: all twelve belong to the man listening.

They again speak of the lost brother as one who “is not.” They say it to the father who still mourns him. Every time they repeat the phrase, the lie of twenty years is renewed without a word. Yet they still count the twelve, as though some part of them refuses to erase Joseph entirely.

The order of their account is notable. In verse 13 they mentioned the youngest first, then the one who “is not.” Here they reverse it: first the missing brother, then the youngest at home. They lead with the loss Jacob already knows, then move to the son at the centre of the governor’s demand. They are preparing the ground for the hard request that follows. Benjamin is about to become the price of Simeon’s freedom and the family’s survival.

wordNotes.term: בְּנֵי אָבִינוּ (benei ’avinu) — sons of our father
wordNotes.explanation: The brothers alter their earlier phrase, “sons of one man” (v. 13), into “sons of our father,” speaking directly to Jacob as the one who binds them together. The word ’av, father, occurs about forty times in these chapters. In Judah’s great speech the word “father” recurs again and again as he pleads for Benjamin for Jacob’s sake (44:19-34).

verses.bibleText: And the man, the lord of the country, said unto us, Hereby shall I know that ye are true men; leave one of your brethren here with me, and take food for the famine of your households, and be gone:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the man, the lord of the country, said unto us, Hereby shall I know that ye are true men.” The brothers report the governor’s terms. They again stress his title, now “lord of the country,” and they frame his demand as a test of honesty: “Hereby shall I know.”

The terms they report are softened. “Leave one of your brethren here with me, and take food for the famine of your households, and be gone.” In their telling, Simeon is simply left “with me,” as though he were a guest under the governor’s care. They say nothing of chains, of the prison house, or of Simeon bound before their eyes. Joseph had spoken of one brother being “bound in the house of your prison” (v. 19). The brothers choose gentler words to spare their father fresh grief.

This tenderness toward Jacob is new. In chapter 37 they showed no concern for how their father would feel; they sent him the bloodied coat and let him draw his own conclusions. Now they choose their words carefully to protect him. The change may be small, but it is a sign that the awakening of conscience in verse 21 is beginning to reshape how they treat others.

The phrase “hereby shall I know” also echoes a pattern in Scripture: God gives signs by which people may know the truth. Moses said, “Hereby ye shall know that the LORD hath sent me” (Numbers 16:28). Joseph’s test, though human, has a similar function. Its outcome will reveal what is true about the brothers.

wordNotes.term: בְּזֹאת אֵדַע (bezo’t ’eda‘) — Hereby shall I know
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “By this I shall know.” The phrase introduces a sign or test that will settle a question. Abraham’s servant looked for such a sign at the well: “thereby shall I know that thou hast shewed kindness” (24:14). Moses offered one to Korah’s rebels (Numbers 16:28). John uses similar language for the evidence of knowing God: “hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments” (1 John 2:3).

verses.bibleText: And bring your youngest brother unto me: then shall I know that ye are no spies, but that ye are true men: so will I deliver you your brother, and ye shall traffick in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And bring your youngest brother unto me: then shall I know that ye are no spies, but that ye are true men.” The brothers come to the heart of the matter. Benjamin must go to Egypt. Without him, there is no proof of their honesty, no release for Simeon, and no more grain.

They add a promise that Joseph had not actually spoken: “so will I deliver you your brother, and ye shall traffick in the land.” Joseph’s words had been framed in terms of life and death: “ye shall not die” (v. 20). The brothers turn the threat into an opportunity, presenting the outcome as freedom to trade. They make the request as attractive as possible. They also omit the governor’s warning that failure would prove them spies, a charge that carried death.

The word “traffick” recalls darker moments. It was used when Hamor invited Jacob’s family to settle and trade in Shechem (34:10), the setting of Simeon and Levi’s massacre, and the related word describes the Midianite “merchantmen” to whom Joseph was sold (37:28). The brothers speak innocently, yet their language carries echoes of their past.

The retelling reveals men caught between two pressures. They must have grain, and Simeon’s life depends on their return. But they know their father’s attachment to Benjamin. Their careful framing shows that they understand the cost of what they are asking. Twenty years earlier they had removed one of Rachel’s sons from Jacob without a thought for his grief. Now they must ask Jacob to give up the other, and they do so with evident care. The moral question has shifted. The test is no longer only whether they will come back for Simeon, but whether they can be trusted with Benjamin.

wordNotes.term: תִּסְחָרוּ (tischaru) — ye shall traffick
wordNotes.explanation: From sachar, “to go about, travel as a merchant, trade.” The verb implies freedom of movement through a land for commerce.
