Hamor offered Jacob’s family the right to “trade therein” (34:10, 21), and the participle describes the travelling merchants who bought Joseph (37:28). The brothers present the governor’s terms as an opening for trade rather than as a threat.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass as they emptied their sacks, that, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack: and when both they and their father saw the bundles of money, they were afraid.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass as they emptied their sacks, that, behold, every man’s bundle of money was in his sack.” Their careful report has just ended when the silver appears. As they empty their grain, each man finds his payment, tied in its bundle, lying in his sack. The discovery at the lodging place was not a single mistake. Every man’s money has come back.

“And when both they and their father saw the bundles of money, they were afraid.” The fear now spreads to Jacob. Whatever reassurance the brothers had tried to give dissolves. The silver makes the whole story look suspicious. Had they stolen it? Had they sold Simeon? Would the Egyptian lord now regard them as thieves as well as spies? The brothers, already trembling from the discovery on the road (v. 28), are confronted with it again in front of their father.

Silver had once marked the brothers’ betrayal. They had taken twenty pieces of it for Joseph (37:28). Now silver lies in their sacks, unearned and unexplained, and it terrifies them. Money they had once wanted more than their brother has become a sign of accusation. Conscience turns even a gift into a reproach.

Some have wondered why only one brother discovered his silver on the road and the rest at home. The money may have been placed at the top of one sack and deeper in the others, or in different kinds of bags. Their later report that they found it “at the inn” (43:21) may compress the events. The narrator is interested less in the mechanics than in the effect. Fear now unites father and sons. The household that had been divided by lies is drawn together by a mystery none of them can solve.

wordNotes.term: צְרוֹר־כַּסְפּוֹ (tseror-kaspo) — his bundle of money
wordNotes.explanation: Tseror means a bundle or pouch, something tied up. Silver was weighed and kept in tied bags. The word is used of Abigail’s blessing that David’s life would be “bound in the bundle of life” with the LORD (1 Samuel 25:29) and of wages put into “a bag with holes” (Haggai 1:6). Each brother finds his own sealed bundle, untouched.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children: Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away: all these things are against me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob their father said unto them, Me have ye bereaved of my children.” Jacob’s grief breaks out as accusation. The word order puts “me” first: it is he who has been robbed. He holds his sons responsible for his losses, though he does not know how true his words are. As far as he knows, Joseph was killed by a wild beast and Simeon detained by an Egyptian official. Yet the brothers know that Jacob has struck closer to the truth than he realizes. They did bereave him of Joseph.

“Joseph is not, and Simeon is not, and ye will take Benjamin away.” Jacob uses the same phrase the brothers had used: “is not.” He now counts Simeon as lost too. He seems to have no expectation of seeing him again, perhaps because he has already decided that Benjamin will not go. The phrase “ye will take Benjamin away” shows his fear that the pattern will repeat. Twice he has sent sons away, and twice a son has not come back.

“All these things are against me.” This is the cry of a man who sees only loss. Jacob reads his circumstances as a conspiracy of misfortune. He cannot see that every one of these events is part of God’s plan to preserve his family. Joseph is alive and ruling Egypt. Simeon is held in safety. Benjamin’s journey will lead to the reunion Jacob thinks impossible. What Jacob calls “against me” is in fact working for him.

The lament reveals Jacob’s spiritual state at this point. He had wrestled with God at Peniel and received the name Israel (32:28). He had heard God’s promises again and again. Yet in his grief he speaks as though God had abandoned him. Self-pity narrows his vision. He thinks only of his own losses, not of Simeon’s plight in an Egyptian prison.

Paul’s words answer Jacob’s cry: “we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). Jacob says “all these things are against me”; God was saying, in effect, all these things are for you. The gap between those two statements is the gap between sight and faith. Before long Jacob will say, “It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive” (45:28).

wordNotes.term: שִׁכַּלְתֶּם (shikkaltem) — ye have bereaved
wordNotes.explanation: An intensive form of shakal, “to be bereaved, childless.” It describes the loss of children. Rebekah feared being “deprived also of you both in one day” (27:45), and Jacob will say, “If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved” (43:14). Jacob accuses his sons of making him childless. The word recurs in prophetic warnings of judgment on Israel (Hosea 9:12).

wordNotes.term: עָלַי הָיוּ כֻלָּנָה (‘alai hayu khullanah) — all these things are against me
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, “upon me are they all.” The preposition ‘al can mean “against” or “upon,” suggesting both that events weigh on Jacob and that they oppose him. The word for “all” is an emphatic feminine form. Jacob speaks as one crushed under accumulated sorrows, unable to see God’s purpose in them. The psalmist voices a similar complaint before remembering God’s works (Psalm 77:7-11).

verses.bibleText: And Reuben spake unto his father, saying, Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee: deliver him into my hand, and I will bring him to thee again.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Reuben spake unto his father, saying, Slay my two sons, if I bring him not to thee.” Reuben, as the eldest, tries to break the deadlock. He offers a pledge: if he fails to bring Benjamin back, Jacob may put to death two of Reuben’s own sons. “Deliver him into my hand, and I will bring him to thee again.”

The offer is sincere but rash. Reuben means to show how seriously he takes his responsibility. But the pledge is unthinkable. How would the death of two grandsons comfort Jacob for the loss of Benjamin? It would only add to his bereavement. The proposal offers the lives of others rather than his own. Reuben had four sons (46:9), and he offers two of them, perhaps mirroring the two sons Jacob feared to lose, Simeon and Benjamin.

Reuben’s history did not inspire confidence either. He had defiled his father’s bed (35:22), an act that would cost him the birthright (49:3-4; 1 Chronicles 5:1). His earlier attempt to rescue Joseph had failed. Jacob had little reason to trust his judgment.

The offer nonetheless shows a change in the family. Reuben is willing to accept responsibility for Benjamin, the very son of Rachel whom the brothers might once have resented. In the next chapter Judah will make a better offer: “I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him” (43:9). Judah offers himself, not his children. In chapter 44 he will offer to stay as a slave in Benjamin’s place (44:33). The movement from Reuben’s pledge to Judah’s self-giving points toward the greater Surety who gave himself for others (Hebrews 7:22).

wordNotes.term: אֶת־שְׁנֵי בָנַי תָּמִית (’et-shenei vanai tamit) — Slay my two sons
wordNotes.explanation: Tamit is a causative form of mut, “to die,” meaning “you may put to death.” The pledge places Reuben’s descendants under Jacob’s power as guarantee of Benjamin’s return. Reuben’s four sons are listed in the genealogy of those who went down to Egypt (46:9). By contrast, Judah pledges himself as surety (43:9), the word later used of Christ, “surety of a better testament” (Hebrews 7:22).

verses.bibleText: And he said, My son shall not go down with you; for his brother is dead, and he is left alone: if mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, My son shall not go down with you.” Jacob’s answer is final, at least for now. He calls Benjamin “my son,” not “your brother.” The words exclude the sons standing before him. Benjamin belongs to him in a way they do not.

“For his brother is dead, and he is left alone.” Jacob speaks of Joseph as “his brother,” Benjamin’s full brother, the other son of Rachel. To Jacob, Benjamin is the only one “left” of the wife he loved. The ten sons of Leah and the handmaids seem not to count in this reckoning. The old favouritism that once fuelled the brothers’ hatred still shapes his words, and how they respond to it will test their change.

“If mischief befall him by the way in the which ye go, then shall ye bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave.” The word “mischief” returns from verse 4, closing the chapter where it began. Jacob pictures his death as a descent, his gray hairs brought down in grief. He had already said he would go down to the grave mourning for Joseph (37:35); losing Benjamin as well would end his life in sorrow.

The word translated “grave” is she’ol. In the Old Testament sheol is the realm of the dead, the grave in its widest sense, where all go at death. It is not portrayed as a place where conscious souls live on in bliss or torment. Scripture describes it as a place of silence, where the dead do not praise God (Psalm 6:5) and “know not any thing” (Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10). Jacob does not speak of joining Joseph in a spirit world; he speaks of dying, of sharing Joseph’s death. The dead rest unconscious, as in sleep, until God calls them forth. The hope of the Old Testament saints rested in resurrection: “God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave” (Psalm 49:15). God promised, “I will ransom them from the power of the grave” (Hosea 13:14), and Paul applies that promise to the resurrection at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:54-55).

The chapter ends in darkness. Simeon is in prison, Benjamin is held back, Jacob expects to die in sorrow, and the brothers live under the shadow of guilt. Yet the reader knows what Jacob does not. Joseph is alive. The grain will run out, and the family will have to return. God is working through famine, fear, and grief to bring Jacob down to Egypt, where he will see his son’s face before he dies (46:30).

wordNotes.term: שְׁאֹלָה (she’olah) — to the grave
wordNotes.explanation: She’ol with the directional ending, “to Sheol,” the realm of the dead. It is the common destination of all people at death (Psalm 89:48), described as a place of silence and darkness where there is no work, knowledge, or praise (Ecclesiastes 9:10; Psalm 6:5). The dead are not conscious there; they await the resurrection (Job 14:12-15). The Greek Old Testament renders the word hades, the term Peter uses when he says that Christ was not left in the grave (Acts 2:31).

wordNotes.term: שֵׂיבָתִי בְּיָגוֹן (seivati beyagon) — my gray hairs with sorrow
wordNotes.explanation: Seivah means gray hair or old age. Yagon means grief or sorrow. Together they portray an old man brought down to death in grief. God had promised Abraham burial “in a good old age” (15:15), using the same word for old age, but Jacob fears dying in sorrow instead. Judah repeats the phrase in his plea (44:29, 31). Jeremiah uses yagon for his own anguish (Jeremiah 8:18).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it take for a buried wrong to come back to the surface of a person’s conscience?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God used famine, a disguised brother, and a hard test to bring Joseph’s brothers face to face with their old sin; their confession shows that his severity aimed at repentance and restoration, not revenge.
discussionQuestions: Why do the brothers not recognize Joseph, and what does that say about how people sometimes fail to recognize the one God has sent?
How do the three days in custody and the binding of Simeon mirror what the brothers did to Joseph?
What triggers the brothers’ confession in verse 21, and what does it reveal about memory and conscience?
Why does Joseph weep in private while keeping a stern face in public?
How does Jacob’s outlook in verse 36 compare with what God was in fact doing behind the scenes?
commonMisunderstandings: Joseph’s harshness is sometimes read as payback; the narrative ties it to his remembered dreams and shows him weeping, sparing, and providing, which point to a test meant to reveal changed hearts.
The brothers’ guilt is not merely fear of being caught; they name the specific wrong, their refusal to hear their brother’s anguish, and see God’s hand in their distress.
Jacob’s words about going down to “the grave” do not describe a place where conscious souls gather; sheol is the grave, the state of death, where the dead rest until God raises them.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the focus on God’s patient work through providence. The famine, the governor’s questions, the prison, and the silver all serve one end: to bring hidden sin into the light so that it can be confessed and forgiven.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: If an old wrong still lies unconfessed, let God’s dealings bring it to the surface now; the One who uncovers sin does so in order to forgive it and restore what was broken.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: Conviction, confession, and repentance: God in his goodness brings sin to remembrance so that sinners may confess it and find mercy, as Joseph’s brothers began to do.
flow: The brothers had hidden their sin against Joseph for more than twenty years.
Through famine and a stern test, God brought the memory of their brother’s anguish back to them.
They confessed, “We are verily guilty,” recognizing that God was dealing with them.
Joseph, unseen, wept over them; his severity concealed a heart ready to forgive.
Christ, the rejected Brother who became the giver of bread, calls sinners to confess and receive his forgiveness.
simpleIllustrations: A splinter buried under healed skin keeps festering until it is drawn out; the pain of removing it is the beginning of healing.
A doctor who presses on the sore place is not being cruel; he must locate the trouble before he can treat it.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you let God bring to light whatever wrong you have kept hidden, and confess it to the One who is ready to forgive?
cautions: Do not present the brothers’ suffering as payment for their sin; it awakened conscience, while forgiveness came freely from the one they wronged.
Avoid making Joseph’s disguise a pattern for manipulating others; his unique role and his restraint served a redemptive purpose.
Handle family wounds with care, since many hearers carry their own histories of betrayal.

reflectionQuestions: Is there a wrong in my past that I have hidden instead of confessing?
When hardship comes, do I ask what God may be teaching me through it?
Have I ignored someone’s distress because it was inconvenient to hear?
Do I trust that God is working for good when, like Jacob, it seems that all things are against me?
Am I willing to let God test whether my repentance is real?
